title: Who was at the Hoofers Club, and what it was for
summary: He names Baby Laurence, Dickie Wells, Corn Bread and others, and insists it was a practice basement for non-professionals, not Broadway stars.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Who was in the Hoofers Club then? Who were some of the people that were --
Baby Laurence, you had a fella called Port Chops, you had what's his name, oh, Dickie Wells, Dickie Wheaton, Corn Bread, Buster Johnson, Ford Marcelin Jones and Buster Bowie, Preacher --
Were these
people all local (inaudible)? (cross talk)
Yeh. Corn Bread --
Were they also performing on the stage anywhere?
Yeah, when they'd get a job, yeah.
Was Bill Robinson a member?

No, this is underclass people. This man, he's on Broadway. Bill Robinson is on Broadway. We were just getting together here. The idea is, because I'd been on Broadway, too. But the point is this is not for those people. This is unprofessional. The people is not so far advanced in the business. That's what this is. Like an amateur night thing. You don't take Bill Robinson and Ray Bolger and Fred Astaire and put them down in the basement where I learned to dance, do ya? They don't belong there, they're not/am I in that category at all;
So what can I tell ya now? That you had to do something to get into the club, the last time you were there they had made --

No, you're learning -- you're learning, you're going to the club to learn. That's what this thing stands for. It's like a pool hall where you learn to play pool. This is where you go to learn to dance or rehearse or whatever you want to do at this place. You understand? Now a professional person don't go in this place for that purpose. No, no, you don't do that, so we don't look for those kind of people in there.
I had heard that some people were considered the kings of the Hoofers Club, the best people there. People that all the kids used to emulate.
Who told you about that?
Chops, I mentioned it to him.
Told you what?
There were kings in the Hoofers Club, like the Tip, Tap & Toe.

No, no -- Tip, Tap & Toe there -- no, no, no, no. This was before Chuck and Checkers came to New York, so how could he tell you about something he heard -- he only heard about this, but it wasn't what he thought it was. Now more than what you think they are now, same difference. He's far now from what he was. He ain't up to par for what he came here. However, this ain't a place where those kind of dancers -- they don't need to go to that club. You don't go there for that. You're finished dancing when you're out on the -- how can I explain it to you? How can I explain it to you?
I think I understand.
No, I don't think you do, that's why I say, how can I explain it?
It was a place to train. What was it, a bar above it, pool hall above it -- it was in the basement of a building, right?

There was nothing above it. Just an empty store above it. I think there was a barber shop above it -- barber shop. But it's a place where you go to learn, it's almost like a hall, it's a place -- they let us use it because there wasn't anybody in it and we used it to practice dancing and anything else we wanted to practice in there, you know.
